Dated this the 22nd day of September 2016
O R D E R

The first accused in C.C. No.167 of 2002 on the files of the court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class - II, Ernakulam filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2(ia)(a)(b)(h) and 7(i)(v) read with Section 16(1A) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short 'the P.F.A. Act').

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class - II, Ernakulam
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.

The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 27.7.2001 at 3 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector, purchased 750 grams of turmeric whole from the revision petitioner.
The revision petitioner was the nominee of the second accused firm.
The third accused was the Trading company, who was the manufacturer of the food item and the fourth accused was its proprietor.
After complying with the legal formalities, one sample was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.

The Public Analyst filed Ext. P14 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standards prescribed for Turmeric whole under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, as it contained insect damaged matters and hence,
the sample was adulterated.
Thereafter, on the request of the revision petitioner, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.

Ext.P15 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standards prescribed for turmeric whole and was therefore,
adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 and PW2 were examined and Exts. P1 to P20 were marked for the prosecution.
No evidence was adduced on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has argued that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P15 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 6 It was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.

The Division Bench of this Court in Rasheed v. Food Inspector [2016 (2) KLT 390] considered the above question on a Robert Lopez vs V.M.Asokan on 22 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/176828475/
2 reference by a learned Single Judge.

entities.text: Robert Lopez vs V.M.Asokan on 22 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Division Bench in Rasheed (supra) held that if an analysis is required to initiate prosecution, there should be notified laboratory and validated method of analysis as mandated under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act for a successful prosecution as held by the Apex Court in Pepsico Holdings (supra).
7.

In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)
(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P15 certificate of Central Food Laboratory cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

Therefore, the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2(ia)(a)(b)(h) and 7(i)(v) read with Section 16(1A) of the P.F.A.
Act, cannot be sustained.

In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2(ia)(a)(b)(h) and 7(i)(v) read with Section 16(1A) of the P.F.A.
Act and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bond of the revision petitioner stands cancelled and he is set a at liberty.

Sd/-
 B.SUDHEENDRA KUMAR,
 JUDGE dl/.23.9.2016  // True Copy // PA to Judge Robert Lopez vs V.M.Asokan on 22 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/176828475/
